title: First Steps
description: Install Claude Code, start a session, steer it, and come back later.

lessons.title: Install & Launch
lessons.description: Get Claude Code on your machine and say hello.

theory.title: Meet your new pair programmer
theory.body:
Claude Code is an **agentic coding tool** that lives in your terminal: it reads your code, edits files, and runs commands, always asking your permission first.

You install it **once**. The recommended way is the **native installer** (first line below). If you already use Node.js, the npm package works too: `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`. The `-g` flag means **global**: install it for your whole computer, so the `claude` command works in every folder.
theory.code:
# Recommended: the native installer
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Alternative: npm (needs Node.js)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

theory.title: Launch it where the code lives
theory.body:
Claude works with the files in the folder you start it from, so first `cd` into your project, then type `claude`. That opens an **interactive session**: a chat where you type at a `>` prompt.

The very first time, Claude Code asks you to **log in** with your account; after that it remembers you.

Want to skip the small talk? Put your first task in quotes after `claude` and the session starts with that message already sent. Kip approves of efficiency.
theory.code:
cd ~/code/my-app                        # 1. move into your project
claude                                  # 2a. open a session
claude "explain the folder structure"   # 2b. or open it with a first task

theory.title: Your first message
theory.body: In a new repo, start by asking for a tour instead of just saying hi. A concrete question gets Claude reading the right files straight away.
theory.code:
> Give me an overview of this codebase: main folders,
  how the app starts, and how to run the tests.

exercises.prompt: What is the recommended way to install Claude Code?
options: The native installer: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Download a ZIP and add it to your PATH manually
exercises.explanation: The native install script is the recommended method; npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code is the alternative.

exercises.prompt: Why should you launch claude from your project's root folder?
options: Claude works with the files in the directory it was started from
Claude refuses to run in your home folder
exercises.explanation: The launch directory sets Claude's working directory, so starting at the project root gives it the right files to explore.

exercises.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
exercises.explanation: Install once, cd into the project, then choose plain claude for a chat or claude "task" to start working immediately.

exercises.prompt: It's your first session in an unfamiliar repo. Which opening message is more useful?
options: Give me an overview of this codebase: main folders, how the app starts, and how to run the tests.
exercises.explanation: A concrete exploration request gets Claude reading the right files immediately instead of waiting for direction.

exercises.prompt: Start a session in your project with an initial task already sent.
exercises.explanation: You cd into the project first because Claude works on the folder it starts in, then claude "..." opens the session with that task already sent.
exercises.hint: Pattern: cd <folder> to move in, then claude "<task in quotes>" to start with a first message.

exercises.prompt: Put the first-run steps in order.
steps: Install Claude Code with the native installer
Open a terminal and cd into your project
Log in when prompted on first launch
Type your first question about the codebase
exercises.explanation: You install once and log in on the first launch, but every session starts by moving into the project folder so Claude sees the right files.

exercises.prompt: Install Claude Code globally using npm. Type the full npm install command with the package name @anthropic-ai/claude-code.
exercises.hint: npm install + the global flag -g + the package: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/…
exercises.explanation: The -g flag installs the package globally, which is what puts the claude command on your PATH in every folder.

exercises.prompt: You're already inside your project folder. Start an interactive Claude Code session (no first task).
exercises.hint: Just the tool name on its own: cl…
exercises.explanation: Running claude with no arguments opens an interactive session that works on the current folder.

lessons.title: You Hold the Keys
lessons.description: Permission prompts: approve, remember, or redirect.

theory.title: Claude asks before it acts
theory.body:
Reading files is low risk, but **editing files** and **running shell commands** trigger a **permission prompt**. For an edit, Claude first shows a **diff**: a before/after view of the exact lines it wants to change. Nothing changes on disk until you say so.

You then pick one of three answers (the wording on screen may differ slightly):
theory.code:
Claude wants to run: npm test
  1. Yes                          → allow this one time
  2. Yes, and don't ask again     → allow this command from now on
  3. No, and tell Claude what to do differently

theory.title: Deny is a steering wheel
theory.body:
Saying no isn't rude. Kip says no all the time. When you deny, add a short note like `use pnpm, not npm` and Claude **proposes a revised version**. The loop is: Claude shows the edit → you read the diff → you choose No → you explain what you want → Claude tries again.

Only choose **don't ask again** for actions you'd happily approve every time, like running your test command.
theory.code:
> No: keep the existing function signature and add
  the null check inside it instead.

theory.title: Start with a task, still stay in control
theory.body: Remember from the last lesson: `claude "task in quotes"` starts a session with your first message already sent. Claude still asks before it writes any file.
theory.code: claude "add a test for the login function"

exercises.prompt: Claude wants to run `npm test`. You'll be running tests constantly today. Which choice saves you the most clicks safely?
options: Deny it and run tests yourself
Approve with "don't ask again" for this command
exercises.explanation: "Don't ask again" is perfect for safe, repetitive commands like your test runner.

exercises.prompt: Claude asks to run `npm install lodash`, but your project uses pnpm. What's the best move?
options: Approve it and fix the lockfile later
Deny it and tell Claude to use pnpm instead
exercises.explanation: Denying with a correction steers Claude toward the right tool without losing the session.

exercises.prompt: Match the permission choice to when you'd use it.
exercises.explanation: Match the answer to your trust: approve once for one-offs, always for safe repeats, and deny with a note when the approach is wrong.

exercises.prompt: Which of these normally does NOT need your approval?
options: Reading a file to understand the code
exercises.explanation: Reading is read-only, while edits and shell commands require permission by default.

exercises.prompt: You denied an edit. Which follow-up helps Claude most?
options: No: keep the existing function signature and add the null check inside it instead.
exercises.explanation: A denial with a concrete reason gives Claude what it needs to try again correctly.

exercises.prompt: Claude proposes an edit you don't like. Order what happens.
steps: Claude shows the proposed file edit
You explain what you want instead
exercises.explanation: Reading the diff before answering, then explaining your No, turns a bad edit into a better one in a single loop.

exercises.prompt: Start a session whose first message is exactly: add a test for the login function
accepted: claude "add a test for the login function"
exercises.hint: claude + the task in double quotes: claude "add a test…"
exercises.explanation: claude "task" opens a session with your first prompt already sent, and Claude will still ask before writing the test file.

lessons.title: Brakes & Exits
lessons.description: Interrupt with Esc, rewind, and leave cleanly.

theory.title: Two kinds of input
theory.body: Inside a session you type at the `>` prompt. Normal text is a message to Claude. Text that starts with `/` is a **slash command**: an instruction to Claude Code itself, like a menu shortcut. Slash commands only work inside a session, not at your normal `$` terminal prompt.
theory.code:
> fix the typo in the README     # a message to Claude
> /exit                           # a slash command

theory.title: Esc: the brake pedal
theory.body:
See Claude heading the wrong way? Press `Esc` to **interrupt** it mid-action. The conversation stays intact, so check what it already did and immediately type a correction that names the right file.

Press `Esc` **twice** to **rewind**: jump back to an earlier message and edit it. The slash command `/rewind` opens the same menu.
theory.code:
Esc        stop Claude right now
Esc Esc    rewind to an earlier message
> /rewind  same rewind menu, as a slash command

theory.title: Leaving the shell
theory.body: Done for now? Type `/exit`, press `Ctrl+D`, or press `Ctrl+C` twice. Kip retreats into his shell and your conversation is saved, ready to resume later.

exercises.prompt: Claude starts refactoring the wrong module. What do you press to stop it right now?
exercises.explanation: Esc interrupts Claude's current action while keeping your conversation.

exercises.prompt: Match the key to its effect.
exercises.explanation: Esc steers without losing anything, double Esc goes back in time, and Ctrl+D or double Ctrl+C leaves while saving the conversation.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the conversation after you press Esc once?
options: It stays, and you can type a new instruction
exercises.explanation: Esc only stops the current action; the history stays so you can course-correct.

exercises.prompt: You interrupted Claude because it was rewriting tests instead of fixing the bug. What do you type next?
options: Stop touching the tests. The bug is in src/cart/total.ts: the discount is applied twice. Fix it there.
exercises.explanation: Naming the file and the actual problem gives Claude a precise new direction.

exercises.prompt: Claude misunderstood you and is editing the wrong file. Order your recovery.
steps: Type a clear correction naming the right file
Let Claude continue with the corrected plan
exercises.explanation: Interrupting early limits wrong edits, and a correction that names the right file stops Claude from guessing again.

exercises.prompt: End your Claude Code session by typing the slash command for leaving.
exercises.hint: / + the word for leaving a building: /ex…
exercises.explanation: Slash commands talk to Claude Code itself, and /exit closes the session while saving the conversation so you can resume it.

exercises.prompt: Type the slash command that opens the rewind menu, so you can go back to an earlier point in the conversation.
exercises.hint: / + what you do to a tape to go back: /rew…
exercises.explanation: /rewind opens the same menu as pressing Esc twice, letting you return to an earlier message and edit it.

lessons.title: Pick Up Where You Left Off

theory.title: Sessions don't vanish
theory.body:
Every conversation is saved. Two **flags** (extra options after `claude`) bring them back. Each has a long form and a one-letter short form that do the same thing:

`claude --continue` (or `-c`): jump straight back into the **most recent** conversation in this folder.

`claude --resume` (or `-r`): open a **picker** of past sessions. If you already know a session's ID, put it after the flag to open that one directly.
theory.code:
claude --continue                  # or: claude -c
claude --resume                    # or: claude -r  (picker)
claude --resume 550e8400-e29b-41d4 # open one session by its ID

theory.title: Switching from inside a session
theory.body:
Already in a session? Use the slash command `/resume` at the `>` prompt to open the same picker.

A typical two-day rhythm: work, `/exit`, then next day `cd` back into the project and run `claude --continue`. The context is restored, so your first message can go straight to the next step.

exercises.prompt: Match the command to the session it opens.
exercises.explanation: Plain claude starts fresh, while -c, -r and /resume bring back saved work in different ways.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday you had three separate sessions. You want the second one. What should you run?
exercises.explanation: --continue only grabs the latest one, so use --resume to pick a specific session.

exercises.prompt: You just ran claude --continue after lunch. Which first message gets you moving fastest?
options: Where were we? Remind me of everything.
Pick up where we stopped: finish the pagination in src/api/posts.ts, then run the tests.
exercises.explanation: The context is already restored, so a specific next step is more productive than a full recap.

exercises.prompt: Complete the commands to continue the latest chat, then to resume a specific session by ID.
exercises.explanation: --continue always picks the latest conversation, while --resume accepts a session ID to open a specific one.
exercises.hint: --continue takes nothing after it (latest chat); --resume can take a session ID after it.

exercises.prompt: Order a typical two-day workflow.
steps: Day 1: run claude in the project and start the feature
Exit with /exit when you're done for the day
Day 2: cd back into the project
Pick up the feature with the full previous context
exercises.explanation: Exiting saves the conversation, and --continue restores it from the same directory.

exercises.prompt: At your normal terminal, continue the most recent conversation in this project.
exercises.hint: claude + the long flag for continuing: --c… (or the short form -c)
exercises.explanation: --continue (or -c) skips the picker and reopens the latest conversation in the current folder.

exercises.prompt: At your normal terminal, open a picker to choose which past conversation to resume.
exercises.hint: claude + the long flag for resuming: --r… (or the short form -r)
exercises.explanation: --resume (or -r) lists past sessions, which is what you need when the one you want is not the latest.

exercises.prompt: You're already inside a session. Type the slash command that opens the picker of past conversations.
exercises.hint: The same word as the CLI flag, as a slash command: /res…
exercises.explanation: /resume opens the session picker without leaving Claude Code, since flags only work when starting claude.

mission.title: Hello, Shell
mission.intro: Time to leave the simulator. Install Claude Code for real and run your first full session loop.
checklist: Install Claude Code with the native installer (or npm) and log in
cd into a real project and run claude, then ask for an overview of the codebase
Ask Claude to make a small edit, and approve or deny the permission prompt yourself
Interrupt Claude once with Esc, then exit with /exit
Run claude --continue and confirm your conversation is still there
mission.explanation: You've completed the core loop: launch, steer, approve, exit, and resume.

cheatsheet.description: Start an interactive session in the current directory.
Start a session with an initial prompt.
Continue the most recent conversation in this directory.
Pick a past session to resume, or pass a session ID.
Open the session picker from inside a session.
Interrupt Claude mid-action without losing the conversation.
Rewind to and edit a previous message.
Exit the session (also Ctrl+D or Ctrl+C twice).
Approve once, don't ask again, or deny and redirect.
